items.proposed_content: Amplification uses auxiliary commuting labels to favor one state inside a spectral average. The same arithmetic structure supports both suppression of unwanted states for an upper bound and resonance at special points for lower growth.

The argument chooses a normalization adapted to the noncompact geometry and a probe point adapted to the arithmetic symmetry. The CM point is not decorative: it converts spatial concentration into a special-value problem with an established convexity scale.

The phase-space lift preserves directional information that spatial density forgets. Invariance sharply restricts candidate quantum limits, but the full-density quantifier leaves room for exceptional invariant singular measures.

A correspondence generalizes a global symmetry from one image to finitely many locally isometric images. The induced operator transports geometric arithmetic structure into the spectral problem without altering Laplace eigenspaces.

Representing a constant-negative-curvature surface as a quotient of the upper half-plane or disk by a discrete group separates local geometry from global identification data: the hyperbolic metric remains the local model, while the group's fundamental domain and identifications determine quotient features such as orbifold fixed points and compactness or noncompactness. This representation gains explicit global models from uniform local geometry, but by itself does not determine spectral statistics or arithmetic classification.

The period identity turns a geometric distribution question into an analytic growth threshold. Separating individual, averaged, and quantum-ergodic statements shows exactly where arithmetic structure substitutes for unavailable pointwise subconvexity.

The invariant torus compresses an integrable family of trajectories into a finite collection of action variables. Quantization discretizes those variables, while projection from phase space explains the visible spatial localization.

Similar chaotic geometry does not imply the same spectral representation. Separating continuous scattering states from square-integrable bound states is required before random-wave comparisons are meaningful.

For a stable closed geodesic on a surface, the cited result organizes an asymptotically regular sequence in the square-root, high-frequency spectral parameter and simultaneously supplies quasimodes whose normalized densities converge to singular arclength measure on the orbit. Reading the spectral sequence and measure limit together makes stability, rather than periodicity alone, the organizing mechanism; negative curvature removes that mechanism by making closed geodesics unstable, whose spectral influence remains unresolved. This comparison gains a precise stable benchmark but does not transfer a construction or proof to the unstable case.

A vanishing law turns sparsity into amplification: if the spectral evaluation mass at a point is supported on unusually few eigenfunctions, those survivors must compensate. This is arithmetic concentration without classical caustics or focusing.
The conjecture selects a one-point amplitude statistic as the observable through which deterministic eigenfunctions may exhibit random-wave behavior.

Norm bounds quantify concentration at different scales, but local analysis forgets the global dynamics and arithmetic needed for stronger control. Multiplicity is a separate obstruction because linear combinations inside an eigenspace can concentrate even when simple basis elements do not.

The inequality transfers a functional-analytic concentration bound into a spectral-combinatorial one. It also distinguishes estimates for a chosen Hecke basis from a constraint on the entire eigenspace.

The source makes theta lifts an adversarial boundary for random-wave heuristics: Gaussian-looking surface amplitudes and exclusion of specified geodesic scars do not control all norms, because on a particular arithmetic hyperbolic three-fold an exceptional theta-lift subsequence has large pointwise and Lp behavior forced by widespread vanishing at an arithmetic point, despite the absence of caustics or focusing.

The source aligns eigenfunction sup-norm growth with L-function growth through an arithmetic convexity dictionary: the general local sup-norm estimate is treated as the geometric analogue of convexity, CM-point evaluation identities convert the conjectured pointwise improvement into Lindelof-type central-value control, and Hecke amplification gives a partial improvement beyond the local barrier together with corresponding nontrivial L-function bounds.

The source separates universality by observable and operator: on arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces, eigenfunction amplitudes may look Gaussian even when Laplace number variance is Poisson-like rather than GOE-like; repeated closed-geodesic lengths then supply a lower-bound mechanism for the Laplace spectrum's nonrigidity, while random-matrix modeling is relocated to Hecke-operator spectra.

Hecke correspondences become different analytic instruments according to how their branches and eigenvalues are arranged: their commuting algebra refines a Laplace eigenbasis, a suitably chosen correspondence separates proposed geodesic singular support, amplifier weights isolate one state beyond the local pretrace bound, and correspondences fixing CM points create the coherence used for lower growth.

Two trace-formula routes turn coherent classical recurrence into spectral nonrigidity. A clean positive-dimensional fixed family at one period produces a localized wave-trace contribution that forces averaged counting fluctuations, whereas on arithmetic surfaces the Selberg trace formula groups repeated closed-geodesic lengths into large diagonal mass in a strongly smoothed mean square.

The source presents a staged arithmetic program beyond full-density quantum ergodicity: Hecke correspondences exclude quantum limits supported on specified geodesic submanifolds by separating and transporting mass, while Rankin-Selberg period identities turn individual equidistribution against continuous-spectrum tests into a subconvexity threshold. These routes constrain different gaps between almost-all and individual equidistribution rather than jointly proving QUE.

At an arithmetic spectral point, the commuting Hecke algebra refines Laplace eigenstates by simultaneous labels; when the geometry is deformed, a different arithmetic datum—a special Rankin-Selberg value interpreted as a Fermi-golden-rule coupling—provides a sufficient nonvanishing criterion for generic dissolution of a cusp form. The supported relation is a contrast between stationary spectral labeling and deformation survival tests, not a proof that Hecke labels themselves stabilize states.
